cites.sentence:
# Tightening Rent Control on Subdivided Units: A Case for Targeted Tenure Reform Over Hard Caps

Hong Kong's 110,000 subdivided-unit households face rents that extract a 15–25 percent per-square-foot premium over mainstream flats, precisely because they are priced at the margin of desperation [D1p1].

The reviewed literature estimates the long-run elasticity of marginal SDU-type supply at 0.31–0.48, meaning a 10 percent cap-induced rent reduction removes roughly 3–5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].

The modelled Hong Kong scenario is starker: a 15 percent cut in initial rents yields a net transfer of about $900 per month to incumbents, against 3,000–4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment—mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4].
This is the welfare trap at the heart of the debate: the households priced out are the same population the cap intends to protect [D6p3].
The elasticity literature distinguishes exactly this: first-generation controls on levels show consistent contraction; second-generation controls show small or null effects [D6p2].
The visible stability in the 2019–2025 index is therefore an artifact of a non-binding instrument, and a binding one would behave differently [D12p2].
The Berlin lesson is precise—caps bind differently on new entrants than incumbents, and the bill is handed to those still outside [D7p3].
Mrs Wong has lived in an SDU for nine years without a written agreement, and reports the 2021 ordinance changed nothing she can see [D4p1].
Mr Chan's worst problem is not price but insecurity: his landlord ended a tenancy with two weeks' notice when he asked to repair a leaking window [D3p1].
When asked what would help most, he does not name rent—he names the waiting list [D3p3].

The NGO survey of 440 households confirms this revealed preference: 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer [D11p1].
The binding constraint is queue length and insecurity, not rent level [D11p1].
Rent caps treat the price symptom of a quantity problem: the segment is tight because the queue is long [D11p2].
Every unit of enforcement capacity spent policing rents is a unit not spent inspecting fire, partition, and ventilation conditions, where harm is documented and immediate [D11p2].

The NGO report supports exactly this combination: tenure security plus a light band on initial rents, opposing a hard cap on the D6 contraction arithmetic and its own survey's revealed preference [D11p3].
First, a band requires survey infrastructure that does not currently exist [D9p2], and a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40–60 staff-years [D10p1].
First, a band requires survey infrastructure that does not currently exist [D9p2], and a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40–60 staff-years [D10p1].
Second, enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail: tenants with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong, or the newest arrivals, are least able to complain [D10p2].
The subcommittee could not identify any enforcement design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last [D10p3].
The elasticity evidence [D6p1, D6p4], the Berlin precedent [D7p1–D7p3], and the landlord exit threat [D5p2]

Instead, the government should adopt the floor-standard-plus-rent-band package already signaled in the consultation [D12p1]: indexed bands on initial rents, enforceable tenure security, and inspection capacity redirected toward conditions.
